title: How disasters change elections
citation: Reeves, Andrew. "How disasters change elections." Reuters, November 5, 2012.
card_summary: Voters tend to reward politicians for taking action after natural disasters, with incumbents seeing increased vote shares when they respond effectively, as shown in county-level election analyses from 1970 to 2006.
plain_english_summary: When politicians respond to natural disasters by requesting and approving aid, they are rewarded by voters with higher vote shares, even though they cannot control the disasters themselves.
research_question: How do natural disasters affect election outcomes for incumbent politicians, and does taking action in response to disasters influence voter behavior?
research_highlights: Incumbent presidents and governors are rewarded by voters for taking action after natural disasters, such as requesting and approving aid.
Presidents receive a modest increase (about half a percentage point) in county vote share, while governors see a larger increase (about four percentage points) when they respond to disasters.
The punishment for disaster damage is smaller than the reward for taking action.
methods: Analysis of all county-level election results for incumbent governors and presidents from 1970 to 2006.
Examination of countywide damage caused by natural disasters in the three months preceding elections.
key_variables: Incumbency status of governors and presidents
time_period: 1970 to 2006 (for study); Hurricane Sandy (2012) as contemporary example
pull_quote: Even though politicians don’t control the weather, voters punish them for the damage it causes. But analyzing all county­level election results for incumbent governors and presidents from 1970 to 2006 also shows that this punishment is dwarfed by the reward for taking action.
